criterion_notes.c1: Yes. Although the study's overarching focus is human contact and exposure to ambient urban river pollution, one of its three primary empirical components (a survey of 1,826 riverbank households reported in Section 4.2 and Table 2) explicitly measures household drinking water sources, waterpoint sharing, supply intermittency, sanitation facility types and toilet sharing.
criterion_notes.c2: No under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, the study does not empirically examine any rule-type mechanism governing water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, administrative discretion, enforcement or utility regulatory structure). Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, it also fails: its empirical analyses examine spatial and seasonal river water quality, zone-level socioeconomic and WASH profiles, and structured direct observations of river use behaviour. Brief contextual mentions that Zone-3 slums occupy government land without legal ownership, that southern-bank residents access DWASA piped water 'legally or illegally' (Section 4.2), that 60 houses were evicted for river encroachment (Section 4.3), and narrative policy overview of industrial effluent rules and river legal personhood (Section 5.2) are unanalysed background rather than an examined governance or legal exposure.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Multi-method primary empirical study combining 12 months of river physiochemical monitoring (13 points) and heavy-metal/biotoxicity analysis (22 points), a household survey of 1,826 households, and 7,900 structured direct observations of river use across 33 days in dry and wet seasons.
criterion_notes.c4: Yes. Section 4.2 and Table 2 report descriptive household water and sanitation service access indicators across the four river zones (piped water vs motorised tubewell use, water source sharing, intermittent daily availability/queues, flush/pit/hanging latrine prevalence and toilet sharing), although in the study's analytical framework inadequate WASH and poverty serve as drivers of human contact with polluted river water.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. Population and units of analysis (1,826 surveyed households within 1 km of the Turag River and Tongi Khal across four zones; observed individual/group river users across six observation sites), exposures/stratifiers (river zone, dry vs wet season, wealth quartiles and WASH deprivation), outcomes (river pollution parameters, household WASH profiles and observed river contact activities) and study design are clearly reported.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is written in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: We designed an interdisciplinary research approach, combining water quality monitoring, household surveys and direct observation of river use behaviour to collect empirical evidence on the state of water pollution, socio-economic proﬁles and water and sanitation challenges in riverbank settlements, and spatial and seasonal variations in people’s interactions with the river water (table 1).

Here we present the ﬁrst longitudinal analysis of the socio-spatial and seasonal dynamics of exposure to urban river pollution, by systematically documenting who interacts with the river and for what purpose, and how these activity patterns vary with the state water and sanitation facilities, river water quality, time of the year and sociodemographic characteristics.

Those living on the southern bank of the Tongi Khal in Zone-3 have access to piped water from DWASA, whether legally or illegally, while people on the northern bank rely on community tubewells. While they have access to an improved source within a few minutes of walking distance, water is often only available at certain times during the day, creating long queues for a limited quantity that is prioritised for drinking and cooking.

A total of 1826 households were surveyed, of which 446 households were in Zone-1, 730 in Zone-2, 510 in Zone-3, and 140 in Zone-4. Data analysis involved generation of zone-wise descriptive statistics and calculation of a multidimensional wealth index through principal component analysis (PCA) of 11 variables on housing materials, education, and asset ownership

Although none of the households are connected to formal sewerage infrastructure, 79% households in Zone-4 use a ﬂush toilet with a septic tank and 86% do not share their toilet with others. The sanitation conditions are worst in Zone-3, with 27% reportedly using hanging latrines or practicing open defecation, with the faecal waste discharging into the river.

raw_response.exposure: Spatial location along four river zones, seasonal variation (dry season including Bishwa Ijtema vs monsoon wet season), river pollution levels, household wealth quartiles, and inadequate water and sanitation facilities driving river contact (no legal, administrative, or governance mechanism examined)
raw_response.outcome: Primary: frequency and type of direct human contact with polluted river water (domestic chores, bathing, swimming, fishing, boating) and river physiochemical/heavy-metal quality; Secondary descriptive: household drinking water source, waterpoint sharing, sanitation facility type, and toilet sharing across zones
raw_response.population_and_sample: 1,826 riverbank households within a 1 km buffer along a 25 km stretch of the Turag River and Tongi Khal in Dhaka and Gazipur districts (446 in Zone-1, 730 in Zone-2, 510 in Zone-3, 140 in Zone-4), plus 7,900 structured direct observations of river users across 6 sites over 33 days
raw_response.rationale: Exclude (E03: Wrong exposure). While this multi-method empirical study includes a survey of 1,826 riverbank households reporting descriptive water and sanitation access indicators across four geographic zones (Section 4.2, Table 2), its analytical focus is on how seasonal river water quality, poverty, gender/age, and inadequate WASH facilities shape human contact with polluted surface water. It does not empirically examine any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor governing water or sanitation service access under either the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading or the plain wording of Criterion 2; mentions of informal settlement land ownership, legal/illegal DWASA connections, and national pollution policies are purely descriptive or narrative background.
raw_response.study_design: Multi-method observational study combining longitudinal river water quality monitoring (12 months), cross-sectional household survey (n=1,826), and two-season structured direct observation of river use (7,900 observations over 33 days)
